Articles

Bullock’s Film Room (subscription)

Commanders Film Room: Jayden Daniels vs Cowboys

[The play described in the excerpt below is the one in the video clip in the embedded tweet from Mark Bullock]

Jayden Daniels looked at his absolute best during the first half against the Cowboys. As a passer, he was processing reads quickly and moving well within the pocket to avoid rushers while still finding receivers down the field. But he also was more prepared to take off scrambling when there was an opportunity for him to do so. He showed signs of that combination which made him lethal at the end of the 2024 season in the fourth quarter against the Eagles last week, and it continued in the first half against Dallas.

Daniels looked sharp early as a passer, processing through reads quickly to get the ball out efficiently.

On third downs, Daniels stepped it up a gear and delivered some nice passes down the field. One of his best throws of the day came from a third and 18 situation.

On third and 18, the Commanders call a dagger concept to the left and have Terry McLaurin running a deep curl route to the right. At the snap, a defensive tackle stunts inside right guard Sam Cosmi. Cosmi adjusts to shove the defender down the line, but he still penetrates and generates pressure. Like on the previous play, Daniels does a good job climbing the pocket but remaining a passer as he does it. He can see McLaurin spotting up on his curl route, with the underneath coverage defenders nowhere near him and the deep safety getting far too much depth. So as he climbs the pocket, Daniels pulls the trigger and throws a strike over the middle to McLaurin, who picks up a first down and more after the catch.

Daniels continued to pick up third down conversions as the game went on.

Fox Sports

The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly From The Commanders Loss To The Dallas Cowboys

The major event is the injury to Jayden Daniels, which will be discussed a length, however the even scarier injury to S Nick Cross. The Commanders hardly have time to reset as the defending super bowl champion Seattle Seahawks come to Landover. Here is what I saw from the game.

Rachaad White- Running Back Rachaad White looked a but off in week one however against the Cowboys we saw the back he was planned to be. White was good running the ball, catching the ball out of the backfield, and in pass protection. Washington needed some dynamic players and White played his part.

Pass Defense-  For all the good stuff up front, the back end was bad. Routinely the secondary was confused, not effectively communicating, and getting beat. Add LB Leo Chenal to that equation and the Cowboys receivers had a field day. A serious decision needs to be made about CB Mikey Sainrisil because he is now the target of every offensive passing attack. Even when Sainrisil was in position Cowboys receivers still caught the ball. He needs a hard reset and needs to come off the field. It would help all parties for him to take a step back and really work his technique and understanding of Daronte Jones’ defense.

Drew Stevens- With so many other issues on the team, K Drew Stevens missed another field goal on Sunday. This one would not have mattered but it shook the belief of the team that they could come back. Stevens has a monster leg but the accuracy needs to be better. If this happens a few more times then he maybe looking over his shoulder.

Leo Chenal- A lot of attention has gone to the secondary and their struggles but LB Leo Chenal has looked outright confused out there.

Commanders Roundtable

Jayden Daniels injury puts Commanders season at a crossroads

Despite how doom-and-gloom things feel right now, head coach Dan Quinn needs to make adjustments quickly. Otherwise, another losing season could put his future in Washington in serious jeopardy.

The Commanders have been riddled with injuries throughout training camp and the regular season. Washington lost star left tackle Laremy Tunsil to a torn triceps injury that will keep him out for most of the season, cornerback Trey Amos is on IR through Week 4, and now Jayden Daniels could be out for the foreseeable future.

Head coach Dan Quinn needs every phase of the team to step up in Daniels’ absence. When Washington trailed 17-3 in the second quarter, Daniels ran the ball effectively and connected with wide receiver Stefon Diggs for a touchdown to cut the deficit to 17-10. He then led the offense into the red zone to close out the half before disaster struck and he suffered the injury.

Quarterback Marcus Mariota finished with a serviceable performance, completing 11-of-16 passes for 111 yards and one touchdown. He’ll need to build on that performance if the Commanders want to have any chance against upcoming tough defenses like Seattle, Indianapolis, and New York.

Athlon Sports

Terry McLaurin: 14 targets; 4 catches; 64 yards; not good enough

Terry McLaurin was held in check for most of Week 1 with 14 receiving yards. After McLaurin was thrown the ball only four times in Week 1, his nine targets during Week 2 are supposed to seem like an improvement. However, McLaurin was only able to haul in two of the nine balls thrown his way for 50 yards. With a cap hit of $18 million, four receptions over two weeks is an unacceptable stat line for someone that is supposed to be the team’s No. 1 wide receiver.

When Stefon Diggs was brought in late in training camp, he was supposed to be a complement to McLaurin, not take over the entire show. Having McLaurin on the outside and Diggs on the inside, Jayden Daniels was expecting a dynamic duo in the wide receiver room as Antonio Williams develops and learns.

Now that Marcus Mariota is expected to fill in for an injured Daniels, first-year offensive coordinator David Blough will need to adjust how the offense will operate. Mariota plays a similar dual-threat style to Daniels but lacks some speed and arm strength. Both Mariota and Daniels tried to take shots down the field on deep go routes but mostly came up unsuccessful. If Blough and Mariota want to keep the team alive, they’ll have to adjust the playbook to incorporate more short and intermediate distance passes while hoping their playmakers can create yards after the catch.

Should Rachaad White displace Bill Croskey-Merritt as Commanders lead back?

The opportunity is right there in front of Washington Commanders running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt — he’s just not making the most of it.

Bleacher Report’s Alex Kay singled out Croskey-Merritt, Washington’s leading rusher in 2025, as the NFL’s player with the “Most to Prove” after 2 games.

“Jacory Croskey-Merritt had a chance to build on his promising rookie campaign and cement his status as the Washington Commanders’ feature back this year, but thus far has squandered a golden opportunity,” Kay wrote on September 22. “Through two games this season, JCM has recorded a pedestrian 106 yards and one touchdown on 28 totes. Most of that production came in the opener against the Philadelphia Eagles, with Croskey-Merritt getting phased out in favor of backup Rachaad White during a Week 2 meeting with the Dallas Cowboys.

“After tallying just 68 yards on nine catches last year, Croskey-Merritt unsurprisingly remains a non-factor in the passing game — reeling in just two catches that have gone for a combined negative two yards. The addition of White, one of the league’s better receiving backs, ensures that Croskey-Merritt won’t see more than a token target or two per week.”

Through 2 games in 2026, Croskey-Merritt’s yards-per-carry average has dipped under 4.0 yards — the unofficial Mendoza Line (which is also unofficial) for NFL running backs.

Mike Sainristil’s ongoing decline pushes Commanders toward a tipping point

After several influential Washington Commanders figures publicly challenged him following their Week 1 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles, cornerback Mike Sainristil laid another dud against the Dallas Cowboys.

And that might suggest the tipping point has been reached with the 2024 second-round pick.

Sainristil has gone from a talented young player to a complete liability. He cannot be trusted, and the frustrations are getting harder to hide.

Sports Illustrated

Should Commanders be thinking about trading for Seahawks QB Jalen Milroe?

As long as Darnold is on the sidelines, Milroe should be safe in Seattle. The team needs him as a backup quarterback behind Drew Lock, but Darnold is expected to return sometime within the next week or so. Once he comes back, there might be reason to trade Milroe.

Milroe came to the Seahawks last year as a third-round pick and had the chance to step in for Darnold if he didn’t deliver as a starting quarterback. Darnold led the Seahawks to a Super Bowl and won it all, so Milroe’s chances of hitting the starting lineup with Seattle are very slim.

He was in competition with Lock to be the team’s backup quarterback this season, but struggled early in the preseason. He was on the roster bubble going into the final preseason game against the Kansas City Chiefs, but he played well enough to earn himself a spot on the 53-man roster.

Milroe is under contract until the end of the 2028 season, which could be valuable for a team looking for an understudy quarterback to step in. A trade between the Seahawks and Commanders for Milroe won’t happen this week while the two teams plan to play against each other, but it could make more sense down the line.

Why the Jaxson Dart and Jayden Daniels Injuries Could Completely Upend the NFL

Two teams we didn’t expect may now enter the race for a top-five pick, which could force tough decisions and affect the whole league

The potential fallout from these two injuries could be astounding if the Giants and Commanders proceed to play like teams that had top-10 picks last year and are now attempting to play 15 games without their QB1. It could not only reshape the fortunes of their own individual franchises, but many others as well. Jayden Daniels missed 10 games last season and the Commanders ended up with the No. 7 pick in the draft (Sonny Styles). Patrick Mahomes missed three games and the Chiefs ended up with the No. 9 pick (Mansoor Delane). Joe Burrow played eight games in 2025 and the Bengals finished with the No. 10 pick, which they traded for Dexter Lawrence II. In 2023, Kyler Murray missed eight games and the Cardinals ended up with the No. 4 pick (Marvin Harrison Jr.). Jimmy Garoppolo played just three games in 2018, leading to the No. 2 pick for the 49ers the following season (Nick Bosa). While there are some examples of teams rising above these circumstances (the Jets, for example, somehow won seven games without Rodgers, pushing them outside the top 10 of the 2024 draft; and the Cowboys won six games despite Dak Prescott missing most of the 2020 season, which placed them at No. 10, though after a trade, they still turned that capital into Micah Parsons), I’m trying to illustrate how commonplace it is for a team missing its starter to be in the conversation for a top pick the following year. Most famously, Peyton Manning missed the entire 2011 season with a neck issue, leading to the No. 1 pick—Andrew Luck—the following season.

Let’s couch something important: We’re operating under the assumption that the quarterbacks available at the top of the 2027 draft will a) decide to actually come out and b) be good enough at the end of this regular season to warrant a first-round pick. Drew Allar, LaNorris Sellers, Dante Moore and Garrett Nussmeier were, at this time last year, believed to be legitimate top-10 options. Two went back to school, one went in the third round and one in the seventh. Arch Manning, Sellers, Moore and Trinidad Chambliss may be the 2026 version of this same situation. 

That said, the Commanders and the Giants now have a top-10 chance of securing the No. 1 pick, according to ESPN’s draft order projection simulator. The Giants have the third-highest overall projection and both teams have better than a 20% chance of picking in the top five. This, at a time when the Dolphins, Cardinals, Browns and Jets are all believed to be at least tangentially interested in upgrading at the quarterback position and finishing around the top five as well. The Jets have three first-round picks, including one from the winless Colts. The Browns have two, one of which came from the Rams. 

Washington and New York both have quarterbacks that, as unfair as this feels to say, can be labeled as “injury risks.” There is a headache-inducing 20/20 hindsight debate, for example, raging about the thinness of Daniels’s frame that has resurfaced from the grave of 2024 draft takes. Dart battled the perception that he was reckless as a runner and appeared consistently in the medical tent in 2025, albeit with only one diagnosed concussion. If he does not play again this season, he’ll have started 14 games over the course of his first two seasons. Daniels would have 26 starts in three seasons if he does not appear in another game this year. 

Analytically, both teams would be filleted if they chose to ignore this and pass up on a possibly generational quarterback prospect in the top five. Again, that’s not being controversial for the sake of being controversial. The value of a potentially awesome first-round quarterback on a cost-controlled rookie deal is a scale-breaker when charting a team’s path to success. If Dart or Daniels were to miss time again in 2027 and either team had opted not to select a top-five-caliber quarterback, it would almost assuredly trigger a change at the general manager position. 

On the flip side, picking a new quarterback that high would be a way to bury the relationship with a young star player, assuredly setting him on the path to seek a Sam Darnold–like renaissance somewhere else in the NFL.

item.title: The Good and the Bad from the Chiefs’ Week 2 win
item.description: Two positive notes and one learning lesson from Kansas City’s win over Indianapolis.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs won an exciting overtime game against the Indianapolis Colts, 33-30. The Chiefs’ pass offense looked crisp, the run game continued to make a difference, and Kansas City got enough stops without cornerback Mansoor Delane to win.

After every win, I like to look at two things that went well for the Chiefs and one thing that didn’t. Let’s start by talking about the impact of nose tackle Khyiris Tonga:

The Good

Khyiris Tonga brings a different element to the Chiefs’ defense

For years, the Chiefs scraped by at nose tackle with cheap veterans, primarily Derrick Nnadi and Mike Pennel since 2019. Both could eat blocks and occupy space, but neither consistently impacted the run game.

This offseason, Kansas City finally upgraded, signing Tonga to a three-year, $21 million contract. After bouncing around early in his career, Tonga broke out with New England by stabilizing its run defense. The early returns have been promising.

The most underrated part of Tonga’s game is his initial burst. He fires off the ball and beats blockers to the spot, especially on zone runs. On the backside, guards have to get around his hips to seal him, which is difficult because Tonga explodes off the ball and chases plays down.

He combines that burst with the strength to control blocks and eat space. Tonga even got the better of left guard Quenton Nelson in the first clip, directing him toward the running back and closing the hole.

That combination of explosiveness and power gives the Chiefs a disruptive presence against the run. Tonga could be especially important when Kansas City faces the Bills.

The Chiefs incorporating play action into their passing game

I’ve written about this before, but I’ve believed the Chiefs needed to run more play action with the skill-position personnel they have. Kansas City’s weapons struggle to get off press coverage and create their own separation. Running play action can help mitigate this, as you can create natural rubs with the run fake and condense the formation, forcing cornerbacks to play off receivers.

The issue is that with the Chiefs’ lack of run game for years, it was hard to get any team to buy the run fake Kansas City would present. Defenders would drop into coverage, so the fake did nothing.

Now that the Chiefs have running back Kenneth Walker, teams have to respect the run threat much more, which has opened up Kansas City’s play-action passing concepts. Mahomes went 14/17 on play-action passes for 137 yards and two touchdowns against the Colts.

One of the first plays of the game showed the impact of the Chiefs’ improved run game on play action. The Colts are in Cover 2, but the WILL linebacker bites on the play fake and gets completely out of position. With the field corner occupied by Kelce in the flat, the MIKE linebacker must choose between tight end Noah Gray’s sail route and receiver Xavier Worthy’s backside dig. He covers Gray, leaving Worthy wide open.

This is a good example of how condensed formations can help wide receivers get free releases. Wideout Rashee Rice motions inside to an F position off the line of scrimmage. This makes it look like he’s going to run block. When it’s a pass, Rice gets a free release. The Colts are playing Cover 1, but the motion gives Rice a leverage advantage on cornerback Sauce Gardner, who has no chance at recovering to Rice on the over route.

The Chiefs ran this exact formation and play twice, including on a critical third down in overtime. Worthy motions across the formation, then Kansas City runs a quick boot to the flat for Walker. The first time, Indianapolis linebackers bump with the motion, giving Walker easy leverage. The second time, Gardner travels with Worthy, vacating the flat. It’s a quick-hitting concept that attacks linebackers who can’t match Walker in space.

The pass offense can’t build entirely around play action, but using it more will make the offense smoother. It creates cleaner receiver releases, slows linebackers against the run, reduces the burden on the offensive line, and simplifies Mahomes’ reads by giving him one or two primary options plus a checkdown. Overall, it’s something the coaching staff should keep refining; it gives them a new and important lever to pull in big games.

The Bad

The Chiefs setting the edge against pin-pull runs

The Chiefs defense wasn’t as dominant as Week 1, but the Colts deserve credit. They ran effectively, added bodies in protection, and consistently used hot routes to neutralize the blitz. Cornerback L’Jarius Sneed struggled in space against slot receiver Josh Downs, but cornerback Nohl Williams and safety Jaden Hicks played well. Without Delane, the Chiefs will be more vulnerable in coverage, but they did enough to win.

My biggest concern was edge-setting. On both Jonathan Taylor touchdowns, Indianapolis used pin-pull concepts to create a wide edge, and the Chiefs struggled to set it.

Downs motions across the play, and Sneed travels with him, eliminating him from the run fit. The center and right tackle pull around the edge, with the tackle easily widening Tranquill. The center doesn’t have to block anyone because Hicks takes a poor angle and gets caught inside.

But the play is really lost on tight end Tyler Warren’s block against rookie defensive end R Mason Thomas. Warren gets enough torque to seal Thomas inside and drive him three or four yards off the line. Thomas can’t lose his outside shoulder here.

On this touchdown, the Chiefs don’t travel the corner with motion, keeping Kristian Fulton in the run fit. Unfortunately, Fulton has to take on Quentin Nelson with a full head of steam and gets pancaked. Hicks can’t beat the center to the hole, Drue Tranquill gets caught in the trash, and Nick Bolton has too much ground to cover.

Defensive end George Karlaftis doesn’t get pinned like Thomas, but he still can’t shed the tight end to make the tackle. You could argue he was held, but it wasn’t called, and he needs to get off that block.

These are only two plays, but they’re on tape now. Teams will keep running at Thomas and Felix Anudike-Uzomah because they’re light, so the Chiefs need to improve their edge setting.

item.title: The Parker Report: Cowboys defense shows incremental improvement
item.description: How did the defense grade out this week?
item.content:encoded:
After coming away with a win in week two, let’s take a look at how Christian Parker’s defense performed against the Washington Commanders.

Team stats allowed

This week, Dallas won 37-20 against the Commanders. Their defense allowed 389 total yards and a 57.1% third-down conversion rate. They also gave up a 99.1 passer rating to Daniels and a 109.1 rating to Mariota.

The Cowboys continue to struggle against mobile quarterbacks, surrendering 69 yards on the ground to Jayden Daniels in the first half before his injury.

The defense did a much better job this week in points allowed (20) and time of possession, although Washington still held the ball longer than Dallas. Some of that is due to the offense’s big-play capability, shortening the field in a hurry paired with their inability to run the ball. But the defense still needs to do a better job at preventing long, clock-chewing drives moving forward. That starts with stopping the run.

Individual stat leaders

Caleb Downs was once again flying all over the field on Sunday. He tied linebacker Dee Winters with a team leading nine tackles, six of which were solo.

Jaishawn Barham and Caleb Downs each forced one fumble on the day. Dee Winters recovered the one forced by Barham on defense, the other was recovered by the Commanders on special teams.

Advanced analytics

Dallas took a massive step forward in the EPA per play department. According to SumerSports, the defense moved up from the 30th ranked defense last week to 21st this week.

Using the same grading system, their pass defense was good enough to finish 14th in EPA per play, but the run defense still struggled with Dallas finishing 28th in that department.

The Cowboys are getting a decent amount of pressure on opposing QBs with a four-man rush, but they just can’t seal the deal. This week, SumerSports has Dallas ranked 18th in pressure rate and just 31st in blitz percentage. But even with that pressure, Dallas was one of four teams in the league to finish without a sack.

How’d the rookies look?

Caleb Downs is as advertised. The rookie seemingly teleports from sideline to sideline, is rock solid in coverage, and has limited his rookie mistakes as well as one could hope for. He recorded a pass breakup on a huge hit and he also quietly forced another fumble this week, this time on special teams. Downs is currently PFF’s highest rated first-round rookie. His ability to do anything that’s asked of him makes him the ultimate chess piece for Christian Parker.

Malachi Lawrence is quietly putting together some nice film. He’s currently leads all rookie edges in pass rush win rate by a wide margin. He hasn’t been able to consistently make contact with the opposing team’s quarterback, but he’s been close. At some point this season, expect to see Lawrence begin to put it all together and finish the season with a respectable stat line for a rookie edge.

Jaishawn Barham is a shape-shifting freak of nature. He’s able to bend and contort his body to get around blockers in the run game. He’s instinctive and physical at the point of attack. This week in a one-score game, he had a huge moment with the forced fumble in the third quarter. And with the rookie wearing the green dot, this defense didn’t appear to have many communication issues. Definitely a positive step forward for the rookie.

LT Overton finished with 15 snaps. There wasn’t enough volume to properly evaluate the rookie.

Final grade: D+

The Cowboys only gave up 20 points. If they were to do that every week, this team might not lose another game. But the point total lies.

After the first drive ended in a three-and-out, the Commanders had their way with this defense for the remainder of the first half. Dallas couldn’t contain the mobile quarterback. They couldn’t get off the field on third down, resulting in a first half 66.7% conversion rate. Without the injury to Daniels, it’s possible that Dallas could have seen a repeat of last week’s second half fiasco where the Cowboys offense rarely saw the field.

The Commanders also had multiple “unlucky” plays as noted in this week’s post game article. They had two touchdowns that were mere centimeters away that could have turned the tide in this game. Such is the way of the sport, however, and close never put a ‘W’ in the win/loss column.

Now in all fairness to Christian Parker and his defense, there were more positives this week than last. Blink your eyes and you’ll miss Caleb Downs flash across the field making a play. Barham had a really solid game, forcing that game-changing fumble in the third quarter. Revel made an appearance with a pass break up. Malachi Lawrence and Donovan Ezeiruaku were around the quarterback all day, but just couldn’t finish with sacks. That’s something you would expect to click at some point this season.

The defense is trending in the right direction, but the question will be just how long will it take to really come together? The offense won’t score 37 points every week. And the defense won’t survive on just turnovers alone. They need to improve against the run game. They need to convert pressures into sacks. And until they do that, every week is going to be a struggle.

This week’s grade was a ‘D’ with the plus added for Barham’s forced fumble at a key moment in the game. Can this defense continue to improve and post the year’s first ‘C’ or better grade against the Baltimore Ravens? It will certainly be a tall task in Brazil against Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry. We’ll see if Christian Parker and crew can answer the call.

item.title: If Saints win/lose vs. the Raiders
item.description: What either result might mean in the Saints home opener.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints will finally host their home opener when the Las Vegas Raiders visit the Crescent City on Sunday. Here’s what either outcome could mean for the black and gold in Week 3.

If the Saints win:

A victory on Sunday would be huge for New Orleans and establish them as a team to be taken seriously in the playoff picture. Yes, it’s early. But the context is huge here.

Both the Saints and the Raiders have gotten off to fast starts. Sunday’s matchup feels like a huge chance for either team to truly prove their worth after three weeks.

The black and gold are betting favorites at home after last week’s resounding road victory in Baltimore. Another win here wouldn’t surprise many, but it would further amplify the excitement currently being felt around this team.

If the Saints lose:

On the flip side, a defeat against an up and coming Vegas squad wouldn’t spell disaster, but it would certainly dampen spirits in the wake of the Ravens win.

With the Saints on home turf, a defeat would certainly be a little unexpected. It’s objectively the easiest game of the year so far, as reflected by the betting line.

A loss would also put massive emphasis on the Week 4 divisional clash with Atlanta on Monday Night Football. If the Saints were 1-2 going in, that would become almost a must-win game early in the year.

Regardless, it feels like the type of game where either outcome will result in a series of overreactions, for better or for worse. Do you think the Saints can take care of business in the Caesars Superdome? Let us know in the comments!

item.title: Chicago Bears Midweek Musings: Whiplash
item.description: Check out @gridironborn’s midweek musings, including thoughts on Caleb Williams, the Bears rookies, and Garrett Bradbury
item.content:encoded:
Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again:

So I may have gotten a little bit ahead of myself tracking the Bears to eclipse the single season scoring record set by the Denver Broncos at 606 points. Ben Johnson’s stated goal and the 59 point showing in Week 1 got me dreaming big. Now, with the Caleb Williams injury and the terrible Week 2 showing, I’m feeling whiplash.

A lot has been said about the Caleb Williams injury and I’ll just say, I was thinking we were dealing with an Achilles tear and how the rest of the season was essentially over. Incredible news that Caleb is looking at a condensed rehab and will hopefully be back on the field by the Green Bay game in Week 5.

Garrett Bradbury might have had the worst day of anyone on Sunday. I know Ben Johnson wants that veteran presence at center, but Logan Jones has the hairline of someone who has refinanced his mortgage – I think he can step in and do the job. To give Bradbury some benefit of the doubt here, the wet conditions seemed to really mess with his game – extra concentration to complete the snap combined with bad footing put him in conflict all day.

The autumnal equinox has come and gone, and we are officially in the fall season. I have failed to complete my summer checklist for the umpteenth year in a row, but this year was particularly bad with the heat and humidity. Good riddance.

I’ve been impressed with the rookie defensive backs thus far. Dillon Thieneman and Malik Muhammad have both played well in their first NFL action. Maybe not a surprise for Thieneman, the first rounder, but Muhammad stepping in early has been a pleasant surprise. This secondary will be tested with this schedule so it’s nice to see early returns on the rookies.

Speaking of rookies, the second Ben Johnson draft class has had mixed results with Sam Roush’s poor Week 2 performance and Zavion Thomas’s lack of snaps. But that’s what September football is all about – figuring out what you have and what you don’t. Remember, Luther Burden was brought along slowly last year before catching fire late in the season. Give these guys a chance.

I drafted Colston Loveland in the third round of the redraft fantasy football league I’ve been in forever. Let’s just say that the early returns aren’t great on that investment.

It sure felt like the Bears paid some additional penalty tax in that game against the Vikings, particularly that late hit out of bounds on the punt return that didn’t draw a flag. I’ve never seen anything more obvious that didn’t draw a flag in my life. And then the guy flopped and it looked like he might’ve drawn a flag against the Bears before the refs picked it up. That would have been an insane double taxation moment had they marched off 15 against the Bears on a clear Vikings penalty, so I guess we should be thankful for that…

After rewatching the game, I came away with the thought that I’d seen that game before, but in reverse, many times. How many times have the Bears played on a sloppy field that reduced the game to a messy field position game, getting the defensive plays when needed, and pulling out an ugly victory? Seems like a million. Bears fans got a taste of their own medicine as the Bears did have two drives that looked like TDs that came away with zero points. The first ended with a Swift fumble at the goal line. The second was disrupted with the injury to Williams where he had the angle for a score before eventually getting a 23-yard field goal blocked. Ridiculous odds of those two things happening in the same game. Bad luck, hopefully that’s the end of that.

As the Bears shape their new identity under Ben Johnson, does it challenge anyone to think that maybe they would be better off playing in a dome where weather won’t slow down their high-flying offense? Detroit put up those great offenses under Johnson in part because they were never slowed by a bad weather game. Just a thought.

It doesn’t matter because the Bears are never going to actually build a new stadium. They’re just going to keep torturing fans with new updates every few weeks that lead to more annoying questions from everyone you run into on the streets and over the the holidays with family.

I thought Tyrique Stevenson and Jaylon Johnson bounced back after their rough Week 1 performances. I also think both defenses benefitted from the wet conditions. It’ll be a real test on Monday to see if these two can be a viable tandem this year.

Pete Crow Armstrong is going to win the NL MVP this year with an incredible season for the Cubs. The last time the Cubs had an MVP was Kris Bryant in 2016. The Bears haven’t had an MVP since Walter Payton in 1977. In fact, they’ve only had 3 players in their 100+ year history to win the award – Harlon Hill in 1955 won one of the league MVP awards, and Sid Luckman took the honors in 1943. The Cubs have had 5 since Payton won his (Ryne Sandberg, Andre Dawson, Sammy Sosa, Bryant, PCA), and we’re not exactly talking about the most successful baseball team here. I need to see a Bears MVP season in my lifetime.

I dug into the history of the Chicago Bears scoring 50 or more points in the regular season and was shocked (well, it’s the Bears so not that shocked) that they’ve only done it 14 times in their history. And they’ve never done it more than once in a single season. I have a feeling that we’ll soon be talking about number of times Ben Johnson’s Bears have scored 50 versus the rest of Bears history. My money is on Ben to eventually win that one.

item.title: Eagles rookie report card: Titans game
item.description: Keeping an eye on Philadelphia’s 2026 NFL Draft class.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles beat the heat and the Tennessee Titans on Sunday. Despite scorching conditions down on the field, Philadelphia escaped Nashville on the back of a heroic Jalen Hurts drive. The rookie contribution on Sunday was small, but here’s what we noticed from the Eagles’ 2026 NFL Draft class.

Makai Lemon: C-

It’s getting kind of funny now. In Week 1, Makai Lemon’s peculiar usage landed him with negative five yards receiving. The screens and shuffle passes were not working for the young man. In the Tennessee game, the Eagles decided to get him on another shuffle pass that lost five yards… Luckily for his box score, it was counted as a rushing attempt. 

Lemon got his first quality target in this game, however, and converted on a really nice 14-yard catch. He broke nicely on a route, Jalen Hurts hit him right in the middle of the field and he caught the pass with bodies around. Those are the kinds of plays the Eagles need from Lemon, especially out of the slot. 

As the season goes on, I expect Lemon’s usage increases as a middle of the field target as Hurts targets that area of the field more and more. While the Titans game wasn’t a stats bonanza, we got a glimmer of hope from Lemon in this one. 

Extra credit: Makai Lemon HOOFED it down the field to help tackle Amani Hooker and prevent a pick six. Nice play, rook. 

Other thoughts on the rookies:

  • Cam Jurgens looked really rough in this game at guard. If the Eagles want to keep Drew Kendall at center, where he played well, Philly might consider benching Jurgens at some point later this season if his bad play persists. Such a move could help Micah Morris up the depth chart behind Willie Lampkin. 
  • The Dallas Goedert injury sucks. Even with the Zach Ertz signing, the Eagles tight end situation looks really rough. Eli Stowers needs to contribute at some point this season, even a little bit. He can’t return to the active roster until Week 5 at the earliest.

The Buffalo Bills are off to a 2-0 start for the sixth time in the last eight seasons, and Josh Allen and the offense are off to a dynamic start, averaging 38.5 points per game in wins over the Houston Texans and Detroit Lions.

Despite the fast start, the Bills are not without their issues, especially on defense, where Buffalo became just the third team in league history to begin a season 2-0 while allowing at least 30 points per game (along with the 1991 Bills and 2000 St. Louis Rams).

Among the causes for concern: Buffalo’s secondary has been picked apart in the first two games of the season; the depth along the defensive line beyond Rousseau, Walker, Ed Oliver and Bradley Chubb has been inconsistent at best; and the defense has allowed opponents to convert on 53 percent of their late-down chances when a stop would clinch a victory.

item.title: Panthers RB Jonathon Brooks needs surgery, out at least six weeks
item.description: The groin injury suffered by Panthers running back Jonathon Brooks on Sunday was worse than initially believed.
item.content:encoded:
The groin injury suffered by Panthers running back Jonathon Brooks on Sunday was worse than initially believed.

Although Brooks was initially described as week-to-week, he will actually miss at least six weeks, according to Ian Rapoport.

Brooks is scheduled for core muscle surgery today. The Panthers will put him on injured reserve.

At this point, it's more newsworthy when Brooks is healthy than when he's injured. The Panthers made him the first running back selected in the 2024 NFL draft while he was still recovering from a torn ACL in college, he tore the same ACL as a rookie, and he didn't play at all in 2025.

Brooks has just 52 yards on 18 carries in his career. He still has never so much as gained a single rushing first down.

item.title: Lions scouting report: How improved are the Jets?
item.description: Diving into the New York Jets heading into their Week 3 game against the Detroit Lions.
item.content:encoded:
With an embarrassing performance on “Thursday Night Football,” the Detroit Lions turn the page and shift their attention to the New York Jets. Lions head coach Dan Campbell has faced his former offensive coordinator in Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson, winning both games, and now he’s facing off against former defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn. Glenn’s looking to improve after an awful 2025 in his head-coaching debut season and keep his head above water.

Detroit enters the contest 1-1, and after a tough loss on national television, they’ll be hungry to get back on the field and right the wrongs of last week. New York is also 1-1 and coming off an overtime loss to the Green Bay Packers at home. The Lions need this win badly to wash the bad taste out of their mouths early in the season. The Jets will want to bounce back from the win they fumbled and regain momentum.

Let’s take a deep look at the Jets and how much they’ve changed ahead of Week 3.

New York Jets

2025 season

  • 3-14 record (4th in AFC East)
  • 29th in points for, 31st in points allowed
  • Overall DVOA: 32nd (30th on offense, 31st on defense)

2025 was not a fun introduction to being a head coach for Glenn. The defense was a laughing stock in the NFL, and the offense had a revolving door at quarterback. Injuries also didn’t help the team’s chances of putting something together. After having successful seasons in Detroit, Glenn got another taste of what it’s like to be at the bottom again.

At quarterback, the Jets had Justin Fields, Tyrod Taylor, and Brady Cook all start last season. Together, the trio threw for 2,385 yards, 15 touchdowns, and 13 interceptions. Fields was the best of the three, throwing for seven touchdowns and only one interception, but he was benched by Glenn after starting 2-7. Taylor and Cook could manage only one win between them, and neither threw more touchdowns than interceptions.

The Jets leaned on the ground game, with running back Breece Hall rushing for 1,065 yards, averaging 4.4 yards per carry, and tying with Fields for the most rushing touchdowns with four. While they didn’t find the end zone often, the unit was their most consistent. Star receiver Garrett Wilson only played in seven games and still finished as the team’s top receiver with 395 yards and four touchdowns on 36 catches. Rookie tight end Mason Taylor impressed with 44 catches, 369 yards, and a touchdown.

The defense is where this team fell apart the most, as they had the fewest takeaways in the NFL with four, all fumbles. The Jets became the first team in NFL history to go a full season without recording a single interception. The best player on defense was EDGE Will McDonald IV, who led the team with eight sacks. With the defense struggling, the Jets traded both DT Quinnen Williams and CB Sauce Gardner to help kick-start a full rebuild.

Overall, it was a disaster of a season for the Jets. The biggest problem was the defense, which allowed the second-most points in the league at 29.6. Glenn didn’t impress and fired multiple assistant coaches after the season, bringing an overhaul to the coaching staff.

2026 offseason

Key additions: EDGE Joseph Ossai, LB Demario Davis, DL David Onyemata, EDGE Kingsley Enagbare, K Jason Sanders, DT T’Vondre Sweat (trade), S Minkah Fitzpatrick (trade), QB Geno Smith (trade)

Key losses: G Alijah Vera-Tucker, G John Simpson, LB Quincy Williams, EDGE Michael Clemons, K Nick Folk, EDGE Jermaine Johnson II (trade)

2026 NFL Draft picks

Round 1: EDGE David Bailey
Round 1: TE Kenyon Sadiq
Round 1: WR Omar Cooper Jr.
Round 2: CB D’Angelo Ponds
Round 4: DT Darrell Jackson Jr.
Round 4: QB Cade Klubnik
Round 6: G Anez Cooper
Round 7: S VJ Payne

Jets general manager Darren Mougey made some big moves via trade to give the team new life, trading for safety Minkah Fitzpatrick and defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat. That wasn’t the only move on defense: he signed more EDGE rushers in Joseph Ossai and Kingsley Enagbare, while also adding interior help with defensive lineman David Onyemata and linebacker Demario Davis.

On offense, more people left than arrived, as the team traded for quarterback Geno Smith to be their starter but lost both starting guards, John Simpson and Alijah Vera-Tucker. The defense also lost EDGE Jermaine Johnson in the trade for Sweat, along with linebacker Quincy Williams and EDGE Michael Clemons in free agency. Even special teams saw kicker Nick Folk move on before getting replaced by Jason Sanders.

Once the draft started, the Jets got help in multiple spots, first on defense, drafting EDGE David Bailey to add firepower to that defensive line. The offense got two good weapons in tight end Kenyon Sadiq and wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr., relieving pressure on Wilson to do all the heavy lifting. New York shifted focus back to defense, selecting cornerback D’Angelo Ponds in the second round and defensive tackle Darrell Jackson Jr. in the fourth. To round things out, they drafted project quarterback Cade Klubnik, who they hope could be their future starter, and added depth on the offensive line and in the secondary.

In the end, this team went hard to address its defensive issues from 2025, revamping its entire defensive line, improving its linebacker room and secondary. The offense could use more attention, but with a coach like Glenn, he’ll believe the defense can do the heavy lifting. After what happened in 2025, if the defense can even be a fraction better, this team can win more games in 2026.

2026 season thus far (1-1)

Week 1: Defeated Tennessee Titans 23-10
Week 2: Lost to Green Bay Packers 20-17 (OT)

Stats:

  • 20th in points scored, 6th in points allowed
  • Overall DVOA: 8th (14th on offense, 3rd on defense, 26th on special teams)

The Jets have had a tale of two games so far this season. The Week 1 win against the Tennessee Titans was a strong defensive showing, holding the Titans to 195 total yards, getting three sacks, and recovering a fumble. The offense was average, with the running game as the heavy hitter, and it scored twice. It was a step in the right direction for the team that only captured a victory three times in 2025.

Week 2 against the Green Bay Packers was similar, but also vastly different in a way. First, the defense played well again, holding the Packers to 199 total yards, getting three sacks, and recovering a fumble. That part is familiar, but the offense and coaching took a step back. After rushing for over 150 yards against Tennessee, New York only mustered 67 yards and found the end zone once. The Jets defense again did all it could to win the game, but the offense could only give them a 10-point lead in the fourth quarter before it all went south.

New York allowed Green Bay to come back in the fourth quarter and force overtime. The coaching issues came in the fourth quarter, toward the end of regulation. Green Bay completed a 5-yard pass to make it fourth-and-5 at the Jets’ 45, and instead of calling a timeout with about a minute left, Glenn allowed the Packers to drain essentially all of the clock, giving Green Bay an opportunity at a game-winning hail mary with no risk.

Then, once overtime started, the Jets made the controversial decision to take the ball first. It immediately backfired when Smith was sacked twice in a quick three-and-out. The defense would allow Green Bay to move down the field and kick the game-winning field goal. It was a massive failure by the team and completely erased all the good they had from the previous week.

So far this season, the defense has carried the team, and the offense can’t seem to get things going through the air with Smith. He’s been accurate with a 70.8 completion percentage, but he has only one touchdown and 462 yards to show for it. Hall has done fair with 131 yards and a touchdown, but he’s averaging just 3.4 yards per carry. While Wilson and wide receiver Adonai Mitchell both have over 100 yards, Wilson’s the only receiver to find the end zone.

Injury notes

Key players ruled out: WR Omar Cooper Jr. (IR)
Key players to monitor: S Minkah Fitzpatrick (groin), EDGE Joseph Ossai (foot), TE Mason Taylor (thumb)

The Jets are a tad banged up entering Sunday. First, they are down rookie Cooper Jr., and now a thumb injury leaves Taylor week to week. Meanwhile, the defense is missing some of its best, with Fitzpatrick and Ossai at risk of missing this game. Fitzpatrick missed the Packers game, while Ossai has yet to make his debut as a Jet. The defense has been doing well without them, but it certainly couldn’t hurt to strengthen that position.

Biggest strength: EDGE

The Lions offensive line will have its hands full again on Sunday. New York has completely overhauled its defensive line, and the EDGE position has grown and gained valuable depth. Bailey has a sack in each of his first two games, and last year’s leader in McDonald IV has added one to his total off his solid 2025 season. They’ve also seen production out of Enagbare, with two sacks as his addition to the line has been noticeable.

It’s not just sacking the quarterback the EDGE players are doing; they’re also helping stop the run. So far this season, the Jets have allowed an average of 65.5 rushing yards per game. With the Lions leaning on the running game a bit with running back Jahmyr Gibbs, it’ll be a difficult test for them to find holes. If the Jets can slow Detroit’s ground attack and pressure quarterback Jared Goff, an upset could brew.

Biggest weakness: Quarterback

While the quarterback position has been a revolving door in the Jets organization for the past decade, Smith is a safe pick, but that’s all you’re getting. Smith did well in Seattle, but struggled in Las Vegas last season and hasn’t impressed much so far in 2026. While he’s taking care of the football, he’s not a threatening quarterback defenses have to worry about. At 35, going on 36, his days of being a threat with his legs are mostly gone.

The Jets have decent weapons in Wilson, Mitchell, Taylor, and Sadiq, but need a better arm to make more use of them. With little threat in the passing game, opponents can focus on their rushing attack to make it ineffective and force them to beat them with Smith under center. Once this team gets a younger, better quarterback, we could see a true step forward for this offense, which is much needed if the defense keeps playing well. You can only be dominant for so long before players get tired and start making mistakes.

Key matchup: Lions secondary vs. Jets passing attack

After allowing back-to-back games of over 400 total yards on defense, the Lions need to wake up on that side of the ball. While the run defense has had both good and bad games, the secondary has struggled mightily in the opening two weeks. Against the Saints, they allowed quarterback Tyler Shough to throw for 410 yards, and they committed four penalties. Against the Bills, the Lions secondary had three penalties and allowed 248 yards, but the mistakes were bigger, with miscommunication leaving players wide open.

The Jets don’t have an elite receiving core, just Wilson as the main attraction. Mitchell has been average since getting traded to the Jets last season, and with Taylor possibly missing the game, the Jets might only have one threat at the tight end position. Detroit struggled against opposing tight ends last week, but containing one is easier than two.

If Smith and the passing attack can pick apart the Lions’ secondary left and right, Glenn could be the first coordinator to avenge Campbell. The Lions’ secondary hasn’t had a promising start, and if they lose this game or it’s close because of it, the team might need to make changes back there to avoid spoiling their season. With extra time to prepare, the defense should be able to make the adjustments needed and slow down the Jets.

Vegas line for Sunday: Lions favored by 6.5

item.title: Broncos vs Rams preview: Denver aims to stack wins
item.description: The Broncos host the LA Rams on SNF after getting their first win of the season. Denver looks to build on that victory.
item.content:encoded:
Bo Nix and the Denver Broncos got that winning feeling.

Now the Broncos will hope for a better showing in prime time than they did in their season opener on Monday Night Football. Up next is Matthew Stafford and the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Night Football.

As with Denver, the Rams got their first win of the season.

In a Week 3 matchup of two of the better teams in the NFL, this could be a fun game.

The Broncos currently sit as +2.5-point underdogs to LA at FanDuel Sportsbook. The total sits at over/under 45.5 points.

Offensive Rankings 

LA Rams: Sixth in total offense (385.5 yards per game), sixth in rushing offense (142.5 YPG), 10th in passing offense (243 YPG), 22nd in scoring offense (17.5 points per game).

Denver: Twenty-fifth in total offense (284 yards per game), 27th in rushing offense (82.5 YPG), 20th in passing offense (201.5 YPG), tied for 26th in scoring offense (15 points per game).

Defensive Rankings   

LA Rams: Seventh in total defense (280.5 yards per game), 19th in rushing defense (113 YPG), seventh in passing defense (167.5 YPG), tied for eighth in scoring defense (16.5 points per game).

Denver: Seventeenth in total defense (330 yards per game), 29th in rushing defense (157.5 YPG), eighth in passing defense (172.5 YPG), 13th in scoring defense (22 points per game).

Here are the MHR staff’s keys to Sunday night’s game.

Start fast offensively

Nix and the Broncos offense finally clicked in the second half against the Jacksonville Jaguars. There was great balance with the run and pass game; Nix was throwing to the middle of the field, and Davis Webb got into a rhythm with his playcalls. Now do that from the first drive of the game and stay consistent throughout. Denver’s offense has the potential to do it; now, just make it happen. Given how dangerous and explosive Stafford and the LA offense are, the Broncos must start fast. — Ian St. Clair

Get pressure on Stafford

We just watched the Rams passing attack without Puca Nacua, and it was pretty scary. The best way to help keep Davante Adams in check (and Nacua if he’s healthy) is to make Matthew Stafford uncomfortable. — Adam Malnati

Score more points than the Rams

Stats and analytics don’t lie. Unlike in Week 1, the Broncos outscored their opponent and remained undefeated. My key to the game is just that. Score more points than the Rams, and they will walk away with a victory. — Scotty Payne

Contain the short, quick passing game

I feel like the Rams feast on the short-pass game, and that is an area the Broncos defense struggled with at times last year. For me, the pass rush will be a critical component of success in this matchup, and they have to show up and put Matthew Stafford on skates. — Tim Lynch

Establish the run

The Broncos gained over 100 yards on the ground against the Jaguars. To limit the impact of Matthew Stafford and the Rams’ offense, Denver needs to be committed to the run on Sunday Night Football and control the pace of the game. I was impressed with Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb’s halftime adjustments. The Broncos ran the ball efficiently under center. In turn, that also helped Bo Nix play better. Achieving this will help them sustain long drives and keep Stafford and his top-tier playmakers on the sidelines. — Christopher Hart

Three NFL matches are taking place in London in October 2026, as part of nine international games being played outside of the United States in the coming months.

Matches are being held across three consecutive weeks in London at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and at Wembley.

The first game sees the Indianapolis Colts take on the Washington Commanders on Sunday, 4 October in Tottenham. Both teams are returning to London for the first time since 2016.

On Sunday, 11 October, the Jacksonville Jaguars will take on the Philadelphia Eagles. While the Jaguars have played annually in London since 2013, the Eagles are returning for the first time since 2018.

A week after facing the Eagles at Tottenham, the Jaguars will then take on the Houston Texans on Sunday, 18 October at Wembley for the final 2026 match in the city. The Texans are playing their first London game since beating the Jaguars in 2019.

The three 2026 matches will take the total number of games held in London to date to 45. With the exception of 2020, NFL regular season matches have been held annually in London since 2007.

The record for the most NFL games in London in a single year is four, in both 2017 and 2019. No other English city has held NFL regular season matches.

Australia hosted its inaugural NFL match when the San Francisco 49ers beat the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 at the Melbourne Cricket Ground earlier this season.

Rio De Janeiro and Paris will also host their first NFL matches this season, taking place in September and October respectively.

There will also be one match each hosted by Munich, Mexico City and Madrid, who have all previously held NFL games.
